newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Up to $400 bln needed to fund new freight ships.
newsitem.headline: Up to $400 bln needed to fund new freight ships.

text.p: Up to US$400 billion is needed to fund global construction of new freight ships over the next decade, but policies in Southeast Asia might hinder lending to the region, bankers and shipping experts said on Monday.

"Investments of between $200 and $400 billion are required to fund global fleet growth over the next 10 years," Ken MacArthur, senior manager at ANZ Bank in Singapore told a ship financing conference.

He said with global trade forecast to rise by 67 percent over 10 years, and more than 90 percent of world trade transported by sea, dry bulk carriers were expected to grow by 38 percent and tankers by 51 percent in 15 years.
Jan Verschoor, general manager of Netherland's Nedship Bank, said $200 billion would be required to replace ageing ships built in the mid-1970s.
"Of this, $13 billion is earmarked for bulkers and tankers," he said.

MacArthur said growth in global sea trade from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) would be significant. ASEAN groups Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Brunei and Vietnam.
Apart from Singapore, ASEAN fleets are relatively small and have a greater growth potential, and local governments have also been pushing for domestic fleet growth, he said.
"Southeast Asia offers a potential for growth in ship-owning and operating which is perhaps unmatched anywhere in the world today," MacArthur said.
He said fleet growth in the region would present natural financing opportunities to banks.

Danny Ding Bong Ho, executive director of IMC Holdings, said bank loans were by far the most important form of ship financing, currently providing about 70 percent of the industry's total financing needs.
But experts at the conference said banks faced not only fierce competition among each other, but also legal and policy obstacles in most ASEAN countries other than Singapore.
There are currently 200 banks in the international shiplending business, up from 150 a year ago, Ding said.
MacArthur said that while many banks were willing to lend, one of the regional issues in financing fleet growth was the obstacle inherent in existing laws and policies in ASEAN.
He said there were also flag and mortgage constraints in ASEAN countries.
All countries in the region operate closed registries, which means that shipping companies must meet certain criteria before they can start operations.
For instance, a firm that owns a ship seeking Malaysian flag registration must have "management which is mainly in Malaysia" and the majority shareholders must be Malaysian, he said.

In addition, as there are uncompetitive fiscal incentives, the government should provide "alternatives to restrictive practices, such as subsidies or lower taxation," MacArthur said. Further restrictions on foreign lenders include the need to get government or central banks' approval before loans are allowed.
